The area fractions below and above the middle vertex height follow from the two edge-intercept ratios. At x=a both formulas equal 1-a and both derivatives are -2; derivatives at 0 and 1 equal zero and match the constant tails. Rescaling a nonconstant affine functional rescales both shifts by its positive height range.

The shift cost is even, continuous and eventually identically 1. At a positive minimizer with a support-exterior or support-endpoint threshold, vanishing derivative and strictly negative derivative on the open support force both thresholds to be exterior or endpoints. Both same-side formulas rule out a positive stationary point, including the middle-height junction. Thus an unaccounted stationary point must straddle the middle height strictly.

Re-derived stationarity in the straddling region as (2a-1)t=a-m. The second derivative is -2/a+2/(1-a), and when a=1/2 the constant branch requires m=1/2 and has value 1. For a>1/2, the thresholds aq and 1-(1-a)q, with t=(1-q)/2, are feasible precisely for 0≤q≤1. Substitution gives J=1-(2a-1)q².

For fixed ordered barycentric coordinates, the conditions on v are v≥-c/b and v≥c/(1-b); c=0 is the only case with left endpoint zero and admits the stated continuous extension. Convexity of c²/v gives the endpoint comparison for 1-J. The c>0 endpoint is a genuine zero-shift cap because v0<1, and the v=1 value is 4λ0(1-λ0)≥4C(1-C)≥8BC.

The two repeated-height cases follow by approximating the vertex-height affine functional with fixed normalized shift; both limiting boundaries have zero area even when they contain a whole triangle edge. For y on the boundary, C=0 and a supporting exterior cap realizes zero. At an interior point a minimizing ordinary cap realizes equality at shift zero; a complementary through-point cap ensures 2f_T/V≤1.

Independently checked the example: 8(2/5)(1/5)=16/25; the null cap at threshold 1 plus the complement of the corner of area fraction (3/5)² gives 16/25, whereas the same normal at shift zero gives 18/25. Two coordinates 2/5 exclude all three vertex-to-centroid segments.
